results.evidenceText: Spatial Reserves | A guide to public domain spatial data and societal issues Spatial Reserves A guide to public domain spatial data and societal issues Home Spatial Reserves About the book About the authors Exercises and data for the book Related sites SM Datum: A Free Browser Toolkit That Meets Spatial Data Where It Is 2026 16 Nov josephkerski Leave a comment As our book and this blog is focused on spatial data, this essay describing a rich and functional set of tools to work with spatial data should be of interest to many. With my thanks to Puneet from SM Datum for this post! “Much of the friction in working with spatial data happens before any analysis begins. A colleague sends a zipped shapefile, a field team returns a spreadsheet of GPS points, a student downloads Landsat scenes as a folder of separate band files, or a planning office shares a KMZ drawn in Google Earth. Each of these is perfectly good data, but each arrives in a different shape. Too often, the first hour of a project goes into converting, re-projecting and repairing files simply so that a tool will accept them. We built SM Datum ( https://smdatum.com ) to remove as much of that friction as possible, in a web browser, at no cost. SM Datum is a free, browser-based GIS toolkit with 16 tools and more than 70 operations, from format conversion and reprojection to vector analysis, terrain and hydrology, remote sensing and print-ready map layouts. What we hope will interest readers of this blog most is the range of data it accepts as it comes. On the vector side, that means Shapefiles (zipped, or simply the folder of .shp, .dbf, .shx and .prj files), GeoJSON, GeoPackage, KML and KMZ, and ordinary CSV, TSV and Excel files. Spreadsheets do not need to be tidied first: geometry can be built from latitude and longitude columns, a WKT column or a coordinate-sequence column, and common column names are detected automatically. On the raster side, it reads GeoTIFF, ERDAS IMAGINE, ASCII Grid, JPEG2000 and SRTM .hgt elevation files. Coordinates can even be typed or pasted in DMS, decimal degrees, UTM or MGRS. Satellite imagery is where we have tried hardest to help. Landsat and Sentinel-2 downloads usually arrive as separate single-band files, and Landsat’s older and newer sensors use different band numbers for the same colours, which quietly produces wrong NDVI maps when bands are mixed up. In SM Datum, the user picks the sensor (Landsat 4/5, 7, 8/9 or Sentinel-2) and receives correctly labelled upload slots, and the bands are stacked automatically. A pre-stacked file works too, and an area-of-interest boundary crops the scene before processing. From there, NDVI, NDWI and NDBI can be calculated, or the land cover classified automatically into water, vegetation, built-up and bare soil, refined with the user’s own samples, and exported with a PDF report of area by class. Two design choices shape the rest of the platform. First, users choose the result rather than the steps. Asking for a watershed from a DEM runs depression filling and flow direction automatically, and returns a watershed polygon with its area. Second, tools connect to each other, so the output of one can move straight into the next: for example, repair a file’s geometry, reproject it, buffer it and lay out a map, with a single download at the end. All geoprocessing runs on the server in projected units, so a 500-metre buffer is 500 metres wherever it is drawn. Because this blog rightly encourages readers to think critically about cloud tools, we want to be clear about how data is handled and where the limits are. Files are processed in memory for each request and discarded immediately afterwards; nothing is stored, and no account is required. There are no advertisements and no daily or monthly usage limits. SM Datum is free to use but is not open source, it needs an internet connection, and uploads are limited to 50 MB per file for most tools and up to 200 MB for imagery. Results such as land-cover classification are useful for teaching and rapid assessment, but they are not a substitute for ground-truthed, survey-grade work. Uploading Sentinel-2 or Landsat bands as downloaded. SM Datum labels the band slots for the chosen sensor and stacks them automatically. The above graphic shows a plain CSV of 16 lakes, dams and towns in Rajasthan, India, previewed in KML Studio before export. Latitude and longitude columns were detected automatically and the points grouped into three categories, ready to download as KML or KMZ for Google Earth.” I look forward to your comments. –Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data The NSDI Strategic Plan 2025-2035 2026 2 Nov josephkerski 6 comments As our book and this Spatial Reserves blog are focused on spatial data, we have discussed the National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI) as an important guiding document for spatial data production, management, and dissemination in the USA many times in this blog space. The NSDI, as defined in the Geospatial Data Act of 2018 (43 U.S.C. 46), is—“… the technology, policies, criteria, standards, and employees necessary to promote geospatial data sharing throughout the Federal Government, State, Tribal, and local governments, and the private sector (including nonprofit organizations and institutions of higher education).” I clearly remember the day I was working at USGS, way back in 1994, when Nancy Tosta of FGDC addressed my colleagues and I with the first bold vision of NSDI. I had a distinct impression that we were not simply creating DEMs and DLGs and DOQs, but were contributing to something much grander and far reaching. The Federal Geographic Data Committee (FGDC) has developed a new strategic plan, Building the Geospatial Future Together – the NSDI Strategic Plan, for 2025 – 2035 . As described on the FGDC pages, the plan was developed with inputs from several sources, “including FGDC agencies, the National Geospatial Advisory Committee, and geospatial partner organizations. The plan expanded the previously more Federally-focused strategic plan and developed a broader nationally scoped plan, designed to encourage active engagement and leadership from multiple sectors.” The pages state that “The new plan presents a bold vision for the future of the NSDI in the U.S., emphasizing collaboration, partnerships, innovation, and technological advancement to create a seamlessly interconnected national geospatial ecosystem that delivers actionable insights to address the complex challenges of our time.” What are your thoughts on this statement and on the rigor of the plan? I like the goals stated up front, “This NSDI strategic plan is guided by three overarching goals: Governance, Data and Technology, and People” – recognizing that creating data is never “just about the data and tools.” The document states that “The overarching vision for the NSDI is that, by 2035, the NSDI will be a seamlessly interconnected national geospatial ecosystem” and I truly hope this will be the case, reducing redundancy in data gathering agencies, providing multiple ways of integrating that data into GIS workflows, and providing rich metadata so decision makers can make the wisest decisions possible. Indeed, the document includes “build once and use many times” and the FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable), which I salute. The application areas mentioned include disaster response, smart cities, health care, supply chain, and others. The document states that “Upon the approval of this strategic plan, the FGDC will begin developing an implementation plan that will include metrics and timelines for the completion of the goals and objectives outlined herein.” I have not been able to find this plan yet, and welcome any reader to point me to it on FGDC.GOV or elsewhere. I look forward to your thoughts, –Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data Tags: AI , artificial-intelligence , news , politics , technology The increasing spatial accuracy in maps at work and in everyday life 2026 19 Oct josephkerski 4 comments The increasing spatial accuracy in GIS and remote sensing work, and even in everyday mapping tools that we use is a fascinating phenomenon. In just a few years, even the details available on ordinary fitness apps, such as on mine shown here, have rapidly advanced to the point of showing individual trees in certain communities (below). I conducted my own survey as I noticed these trees, and in most cases, the locations were accurate, and those symbolized on the map as larger symbols were indeed larger than those nearby, on the ground. Could the app be using a local tree data set from this community? In this community where I was walking, I also noticed that the alleyways were shown on the basemap in my fitness app; for example, at the location I was standing, at the blue dot, below. Was there an alley there? I conducted some field tests: Alley shown on the map to the west of where I was standing. … and sure, enough, there was indeed an alleyway there! The alley shown on the basemap in the above fitness app. Contrast the above high resolution base map with my post using the same fitness app, comparing 2012 and 2015, here in my “walking on water” essay: Walking on Water? Revisiting Reflections on Resolution and Scale | Spatial Reserves This 2012 and 2015 coarse base map seems ancient, but it was only from the last decade! 2012: 2015: Such developments make tools in use everyday more interesting and more suited to our needs (is the bus really only 1 minute and 20 seconds from here? Sure enough, 1 minute and 20 seconds later, here it is at my stop!). Yet with increasing spatial and attribute accuracy is accompanied by increasing potential for treading on one’s location privacy. Indeed, is any of our locations truly private these days? See my related recent posts: Here, about my colleague who tried to be “off camera” in the community: Location Privacy: The plethora of cameras in the community | Spatial Reserves And blurring of images in ground photographs: Location Privacy: Update on Blurring of Images in Ground Photographs | Spatial Reserves And while inside buildings: Location Privacy While Shopping at Physical Stores | Spatial Reserves What are your thoughts on this topic as we head into the latter part of the 2020s? And for the educators reading this blog, how do you teach about this issue? In which courses do you do so? — Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data A Chatbot for a GIS Hub’s Data Library 2026 5 Oct josephkerski Leave a comment Examining the capabilities of GIS libraries and the implications for future use of spatial data has long been a theme of this blog. Another recurring theme in this blog has been the developments and implications of AI tools on GIS. The Cobb County Georgia ArcGIS Hub site is a good example of both a wonderfully functional data library as well as offering an innovative use of AI in obtaining meaningful information. A GIS chatbot was developed by the GIS analysts for Cobb County Georgia, to handle both public and internal inquiries in real time. To overcome the fact that most Large Language Models (LLMs) don’t have expertise in specific domains, the Cobb County staff developed something called Retrieval-Augmented Generation, which obtains relevant, up-to-date information from their GIS dataset and provides it as context for the model, which improves response quality and reliability. Here is the data served to the public via the county’s GIS hub site: https://geo-cobbcountyga.hub.arcgis.com/pages/get-data For more information, see my Esri colleague Jim Baumann’s article about the site and its capabilities, and why and how they developed the Chatbot capabilities, here: Get to Know Cobb County’s GIS Chatbot | Spring 2026 | ArcUser According to the above article, analyst Chunguang Zhang, said, “The GIS chatbot answers frequent GIS-related questions and queries, which reduces the need for human interaction and support. This improves response times and ensures consistency in the response. It also allows staff to quickly retrieve zoning information, parcel verification, address validation, and GIS application data.” Thus, the Chatbot is to serve both the internal staff as well as the general public. I especially like this part: “In developing the GIS chatbot, Zhang compiled years of resident inquiries and staff responses from GIS-related emails for training purposes. To ensure the consistency of the chatbot’s response, he leveraged ChatGPT to generate three similar variations of each question while keeping exactly the same answer. This ensured uniform and accurate responses every time.” I say “bravo” to this clever work. As an educator, I also appreciate the array of educational items on the county’s GIS site, too, such as these geospatial tools for the classroom and this “What is GIS?” story map: Intro to Geography & GIS in Cobb County | Cobb County GIS Hub Site . I anticipate AI tools becoming embedded in many ArcGIS Hub sites and other spatial data libraries. It has the potential to narrow the results that a data user can find, and potentially hinder the creative habits that humans have developed in the data acquisition skills building. But, done right, it also has the potential to enhance what could be found on such sites, as well as reduce data searching time for the analyst, allowing more time for analysis and synthesis, and other tasks. What is your reaction to the above? –Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data A Fully Online Course based on GIS and Society is now freely available 2026 21 Sep josephkerski 2 comments Would you like to take a course based on the following 3 important and relevant themes? Where to find spatial data . How to critically evaluate that data . Societal issues surrounding data: Copyright, data quality, ethics, location privacy, AI, and others. A course focusing on the above 3 themes is now freely available via a self-paced online course, linked below. This course contains selected, pertinent content of our book and blog Spatial Reserves; and in addition, hands-on engaging exercises where you grapple with concepts of: Scale Uncertainty Ethics and other issues in a decision-making GIS environment. I have rigorously tested, taught, refined, and evaluated this course in higher education full-semester settings, short courses, online and face-to-face, in a wide variety of settings for a wide diversity of GIS data users and analysts in multiple locations around the world. The course is served as a story map collection, available here. Here is a playlist of the course videos: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLL_rej_JJ9qk&si=rIdPRLtIyLG04Pd9 It is also described in the following essay: https://community.esri.com/t5/education-blog/a-new-complete-course-in-data-gis-and-society/ba-p/1402213 Plus, the course is also served as an ArcGIS Experience, here: https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/726bab5044f74bb4a1de4965de679c7d This course invites learners to work with real data to solve problems and foster skills through a set of readings, hands-on activities, discussions, quizzes, and a final project.  I also invite instructors who seek to incorporate meaningful data and discussion about data in their courses to use all or part of this course in their own courses and programs. The Course is served as a story map collection and as an ArcGIS Experience (both shown above). Course Description:   Geospatial data are the foundation upon which GIS and spatial analysis rests. As GIS has matured, the challenge has evolved from generating data to managing the enormous volume of data from government agencies, nonprofit organizations, and industry, and increasingly, from ordinary citizens through citizen science and volunteered geographic information efforts. Key to working with this volume of data are essential issues such as privacy, copyright, public domain, cost recovery, metadata standards, and data quality that GIS professionals must grapple with to be effective in the 21st Century. This class discusses and applies these issues and works with a rich array of data sources to enable effective decision-making in a Geographic Information System.  The prerequisite for this course is an introductory GIS course or similar GIS course and/or work experience. Course Questions: The course is focused on three questions: 1.  How can I find geospatial data for my projects? 2.  How do I know if I can trust the geospatial data that I find?   In other words, how can I assess geospatial data quality?  3.  How can I consider societal issues surrounding geospatial data and tools, including copyright, location privacy, ethics, symbology, classification methods, map projections, and others?  Course Philosophy:  Four philosophies run through the course: 1.  Data is the foundation for all mapping, analysis, and decision-making that stems from that mapping and analysis.  Thus, data and data quality are vitally important to continually ask questions about, to seek, and to assess. 2.  Scale matters.  Patterns and relationships may exist at one scale and not another, and vice versa.  The scale at which you are conducting your analysis and the scale at which your data has been collected and published have great influences on the patterns that you will see, and the patterns that will remain hidden. 3.  You will encounter data that is understandable, and data that is confusing.    You will encounter data portals that are easy-to-use, and others that are difficult.  This is intentional:  The course instructor is not cleaning up any of the data or the data sites.  You will encounter the exact same thing in the workplace, and learning how to deal with geo-data challenges is central to the objectives of this course. 4.  Today’s GIS tools and open data portals are easier to use than ever before.  However, learning GIS is not just learning software interfaces and where data are located.  Central to successful use of GIS and to this course is cultivating a  healthy critical view of data and of GIS tools–recognizing their benefits, and also their limitations.   Course Themes: Weekly themes of this course include: Week 1:  Spatial data and the public domain.    GIS in our everyday lives.   Week 2:  Vector data model and data, portals, data quality.  Week 3:  Raster data model and data, portals, location privacy.  Week 4:  Data costs, local data access.  Week 5:  Metadata and standards.  National and state data portals.   Week 6:   National and international data infrastructures and initiatives.   Week 7:  Data policies.   Week 8:  Crowdsourced data.  Data disclaimers.  Week 9:  Cloud computing and GIS.  Software as a service.  Week 10:  The future of public domain spatial data.     Course Prerequisites and History: This 10 week online course was created for a graduate program inside a university GIS program.  This course is meant to follow an introductory course covering basic GIS skills.  I have taught, assessed, and improved this course each year over the span of over 20 years and am happy to share it with the community.  The course was originally taught face-to-face, then taught online via a Learning Management System (LMS), and then moved into a space so that you can access it, above.   Course Issues, Skills, Data Sets, and Portals: Major issues addressed include:   Data sources, data representation and models, data quality, metadata, spatial data input and output, spatial analysis, location privacy, copyright, streaming vs. downloading data, on premises servers vs. open access, spatial data serving policy.   Major skills addressed include:  spatial data management, analyzing tabular information, data input and querying, locating spatial data, assessing spatial data, formatting spatial data, projecting, georeferencing, geocoding, overlay and proximity, merging, raster data analysis, preparing 3D visualizations, making decisions with GIS and data.  Major data sets used in this course:   The ArcGIS

results.pageDescription: Allowing scraped content to be used for all "advertising and business products" is a substantial expansion of Meta's permissions.
results.evidenceText: Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes | Nieman Journalism Lab Get Nieman Lab in your inbox. All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Subscribe another address Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions. Meta-owned platforms include Facebook, WhatsApp, Oculus, Threads, Instagram, and Messenger. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 17, 2026, 2:30 p.m. RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models. In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts. On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then. “I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'” Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.” Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place. As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold): You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products . Here’s the original text : You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains , web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train , and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements . The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 ★ Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Adding this language to more general terms of service, and allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products,” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s scraping permissions. A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “ Ad Creative Generative AI Terms ” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand. Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements. “[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.” University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house. “You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 At least three journalism organizations have publicly raised concerns about the forthcoming terms as a result of Nieman Lab’s reporting. Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “ scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power .” The United Kingdom News Media Association , the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene. “This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber . “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.” The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “ outrageous and probably illegal .” “The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” This story has been updated to include comments from Meta. Subscribe another address Sinclair’s new Substack repackages its local TV reporting into a video podcast Link axios.com ↗ Posted by Hanaa' Tameez October 7, 2026 “How young is too young for a life in prison?” “SpaceX debris is washing ashore. Who’s responsible?” “Why schools get paid even when students fail.” Those are the top headlines so far on Sinclair Broadcasting Group’s new Substack publication, The National Press , launched this week. The National Press repackages some of the top stories from Sinclair’s 178 local news stations — which employ around 1,200 journalists — into a daily, 30-minute broadcast-style show. The program is hosted by former Newsmax and Christian Cable Network anchor Lyndsay Keith , who summarizes the stories and interviews the local journalists who first reported them. In the videos, Keith sits at a desk with a microphone; the dimly lit background is illuminated just enough to make out two American flags in a mug. (It gives off a true-crime YouTube podcast vibe.) As Axios’s Sara Fischer noted on Tuesday , Sinclair has long been accused of conservative bias in its local news operation. The National Press is launching in partnership with New Media, the company behind Bari Weiss’s The Free Press, and the two publications look somewhat alike (in part because they both run on Substack). New Media staffers will help create the content and maintain the site and the company will take a portion of Sinclair’s revenue from Substack, Fischer reported. The National Press is currently free to access, but has paid tiers that include ad-free viewing, community chat access, and merch. Subscriptions start at $5 per month or $50 per year. The five posts on the site so far have between seven and 14 likes each. Wednesday’s episode focuses on a story about how Michigan is reconsidering lifetime sentences for people sentenced between the ages of 18 and 20. It also tackles AI regulation debates in Congress, drawing on reporting by Capitol Hill reporter Ahtra Elnashar. The show doesn’t appear to be filmed in one take like a true TV news broadcast (Keith is first seen in a black blazer, then a brown one, before switching back to black by the end of the video). Another video, “ Worth Noticing: School Bus Incidents ,” is just two minutes long and compiles stories of school bus crashes from around the country. From the text accompanying the video: We trust school buses to get our kids from the safety of our homes to school every day. So why are we seeing so many serious injuries and incidents? Is this simply a string of unrelated tragedies? Are staffing shortages the problem here? Training gaps? Weak safety protocols? We’re going to be following these stories. Have you seen incidents like this in your community? Is this something that is keeping you awake at night? Because these stories are horrific; we’re talking about every parent’s nightmare. The National Press isn’t Sinclair’s first effort to reach a younger, video-first audience. In 2015, it launched millennial-focused news site Circa , which shuttered four years later. U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline Link parliamentlive.tv ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck , Hanaa' Tameez October 21, 2026 The U.K. competition and consumer protection authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss its new commercial terms of service. On Tuesday, Will Hayter , the executive director for digital markets at the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), shared the update during a session of the communications and digital committee of British Parliament , after a member of the House of Lords pressed him about Meta’s new terms. Hayter said he scheduled a meeting with the tech giant today to seek clarity on the new terms, though the CMA declined to provide any further details. RELATED ARTICLE Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Andrew Deck October 17, 2026 Last week, Nieman Lab broke the news that the terms would permit mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. The new terms are slated to take effect on October 30, and there is currently no option to opt out. Virtually every news organization owns at least one Meta business account. “Are you going to pause the deadline? I mean, [it’s in] a week,” Veronica Wadley, Baroness Fleet and a former editor of the Evening Standard, said during the session of Parliament. “You know this includes almost every U.K. news publisher and it is clearly uncompetitive leverage of Meta’s strategic market position.” In the same session, Sarah Cardell , the CEO of CMA, said the authority had limited intervention options because it has not formally designated Meta as an “entrenched market power” (something it has done in the past for Google and Apple ). Cardell said other competition enforcement actions are a possibility, but the CMA is “urgently” seeking more information from Meta before making any judgment. Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 ★ U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Over the weekend, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping. A Meta spokesperson said on Saturday that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. “Does Meta think we can’t read?” Theo Bamber , chief executive of the U.K.’s News Media Association, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Monday. “We know you’ve taken the word ‘train’ out but changing it to ‘develop’ isn’t fooling anyone.” News publisher associations across Europe have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect next week. On Tuesday, two major German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review had been conducted. Together, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers represent more than 9,000 media brands across Europe. RELATED ARTICLE Meet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAI Andrew Deck February 20, 2025 “Meta intends to automatically capture, copy, and store the complete websites and archives of publishers and analyze them for its own automated and non-automated commercial products,” reads a joint statement from the associations . “This makes access to Meta’s platforms contingent on the free surrender of the entire digital publishing product. This is blatant theft.” The statement alleges that Meta’s new terms could be in violation of the E.U. Digital Markets Act, which was passed in 2022 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region. The publishers cited a specific clause that guarantees “fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory general conditions of access for business users.” The uproar from European publishers echoes similar opposition to the new terms from major U.S. publisher associations. Jason Kint, the CEO of Digital Content Next, has been vocal about his skepticism of the new terms since Nieman Lab’s story broke last week. “Meta’s supposed Friday night correction to its new commercial terms is a farce,” he wrote in a statement published on Tuesday. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.” Get Nieman Lab’s Daily Digest The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon. results.evidenceText: GeoPandas 1.2.1.dev0.dev+g199fc53c8 — GeoPandas 1.2.1.dev0+g199fc53c8.d20260928 documentation Skip to main content Back to top Ctrl + K System Settings Light Dark GitHub GeoPandas 1.2.1.dev0.dev+g199fc53c8 # GeoPandas is an open source project to make working with geospatial data in python easier. GeoPandas extends the datatypes used by pandas to allow spatial operations on geometric types. Geometric operations are performed by shapely . Geopandas further depends on pyogrio for file access and matplotlib for plotting. Description # The goal of GeoPandas is to make working with geospatial data in python easier. It combines the capabilities of pandas and shapely, providing geospatial operations in pandas and a high-level interface to multiple geometries to shapely. GeoPandas enables you to easily do operations in python that would otherwise require a spatial database such as PostGIS. results.evidenceText: spaCy · Industrial-strength Natural Language Processing in Python Get things done spaCy is designed to help you do real work — to build real products, or gather real insights. The library respects your time, and tries to avoid wasting it. It's easy to install, and its API is simple and productive. Blazing fast spaCy excels at large-scale information extraction tasks. It's written from the ground up in carefully memory-managed Cython. If your application needs to process entire web dumps, spaCy is the library you want to be using. Awesome ecosystem Since its release in 2015, spaCy has become an industry standard with a huge ecosystem. Choose from a variety of plugins, integrate with your machine learning stack and build custom components and workflows. Edit the code & try spaCy spaCy v 3.7 · Python 3 · via Binder run Features Support for 75 + languages 84 trained pipelines for 25 languages Multi-task learning with pretrained transformers like BERT Pretrained word vectors State-of-the-art speed Production-ready training system Linguistically-motivated tokenization Components for named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, sentence segmentation, text classification , lemmatization, morphological analysis, entity linking and more Easily extensible with custom components and attributes Support for custom models in PyTorch , TensorFlow and other frameworks Built in visualizers for syntax and NER Easy model packaging , deployment and workflow management Robust, rigorously evaluated accuracy NEW Large Language Models: Integrating LLMs into structured NLP pipelines The spacy-llm package integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) into spaCy, featuring a modular system for fast prototyping and prompting , and turning unstructured responses into robust outputs for various NLP tasks, no training data required. Learn more From the makers of spaCy Prodigy: Radically efficient machine teaching Prodigy is an annotation tool so efficient that data scientists can do the annotation themselves, enabling a new level of rapid iteration. Whether you're working on entity recognition, intent detection or image classification, Prodigy can help you train and evaluate your models faster. Try it out Reproducible training for custom pipelines spaCy v3.0 introduces a comprehensive and extensible system for configuring your training runs . Your configuration file will describe every detail of your training run, with no hidden defaults, making it easy to rerun your experiments and track changes. You can use the quickstart widget or the init config command to get started, or clone a project template for an end-to-end workflow. results.pageTitle: Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project
results.evidenceText: Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project ¶ Introduction ¶ QGIS is a user friendly Open Source Geographic Information System (GIS) that runs on Linux, Unix, macOS, and Windows. QGIS supports vector, raster, and database formats. QGIS is licensed under the GNU General Public License. QGIS lets you browse and create map data on your computer. It supports many common spatial data formats (e.g. ESRI ShapeFile, GeoPackage, PostGIS, geotiff). QGIS supports plugins to do things like display tracks from your GPS. QGIS is Open Source software and it is free of cost ( download here ). We welcome contributions from our user community in the form of code contributions, bug fixes, bug reports, contributed documentation, advocacy and supporting other users on our mailing lists and forums. Financial contributions are also welcome. QGIS source code is available at https://github.com/qgis/QGIS . There is also a C++ version of the API documentation available. Versions of the API ¶ Documentation for master: https://qgis.org/pyqgis/master Documentation for current stable 4.2: https://qgis.org/pyqgis/4.2 Documentation for current LTR 3.44: https://qgis.org/pyqgis/3.44 See Backwards Incompatible Changes for information about incompatible changes to API between releases. Earlier versions of the documentation are also available as downloads: 4.0 , 3.42 , 3.40 , 3.38 , 3.36 , 3.34 , 3.32 , 3.30 , 3.28 , 3.26 , 3.24 , 3.22 , 3.20 , 3.18 , 3.16 , 3.14 , 3.12 , 3.10 , 3.8 , 3.6 , 3.4 , 3.2 , 3.0 . Communication channels ¶ For support we encourage you to join our mailing lists for users and developers. Some QGIS users and developers can also often be found in channels such as Matrix, Telegram,… Bug Reporting ¶ If you think you have found a bug in the documentation, please report it using our bug tracker . When reporting bugs, please be available to follow up on your initial report. results.pageDescription: From Data to Viz leads you to the most appropriate graph for your data. It links to the code to build it and lists common caveats you should avoid.
results.evidenceText: From data to Viz | Find the graphic you need What kind of data do you have? Pick the main type using the buttons below. Then let the decision tree guide you toward your graphic possibilities. Alternatively, check the complete decision tree . Numeric Categoric Num & Cat Maps Time series Network Swipe sideways to see the whole tree → Data Story From Data to Viz provides a decision tree based on input data format. This tree leads to twenty formats representing the most common dataset types. For each, an example of analysis based on real-life data is provided using the R programming language . Caveats The best way to visualize data efficiently is probably to avoid the most common mistakes. From Data to Viz offers you a gallery of common caveats . Order your data When displaying the value of several entities, ordering it makes it way more insightful. To cut or not to cut? Cutting the Y axis is one of the most controversial practices in data viz. See why. The spaghetti chart A line graph with too many lines becomes unreadable: it is called a spaghetti graph. From September 8–11, 2026 , Brno became a meeting place for the European and international cartographic community. More than 260 participants came together for four days of presentations, keynote lectures, workshops, poster sessions, discussions, and networking. Under the motto “Let’s transform cartography together” , EuroCarto 2026 provided a platform for researchers, professionals, and students to exchange ideas, share new developments, and discuss the future of cartography, geovisualization, and spatial technologies. The conference began on Tuesday, September 8, with pre-conference workshops , followed by the Opening Ceremony and Welcome Reception in the evening. Organized by the Czech Cartographic Society under the patronage of the International Cartographic Association , EuroCarto 2026 welcomed participants from across Europe and beyond, bringing together a diverse community with a shared interest in the transformation and future of cartography. Subscribe another address A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results Link idjc.syracuse.edu ↗ Posted by Sarah Scire October 15, 2026 Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received? It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could. In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories. The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.) The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr , director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough. “Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.” “The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.” RELATED ARTICLE Searching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalism Angie Drobnic Holan April 27, 2023 At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject. When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence. In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio ) more often than reporter-named accounts. The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here . results.title: ArchieML
results.pageDescription: ArchieML is a text format optimized for human writability. It was designed for users unfamiliar with existing serialization formats, and defines a forgiving, incremental parser that does not throw syntax errors.
results.evidenceText: Archie Markup Language (ArchieML) ArchieML ArchieML is a structured text format optimized for human writability. Resources Demo Usage Sandbox Spec Structured text, for an unstructured world. What is Archie Markup Language? ArchieML (or "AML") was created at The New York Times to make it easier to write and edit structured text on deadline that could be rendered in web pages, or more specifically, rendered in interactive graphics. One of the main goals was to make it easy to tag text as data, without having type a lot of special characters. Another goal was to allow the document to contain lots of notes and draft text that would not be read into the data. And finally, because we make extensive use of Google Documents's concurrent-editing features — while working on a graphic, we can have several reporters, editors and developers all pouring information into a single document — we wanted to have a format that could survive being edited by users who may never have seen ArchieML or any other markup language at all before. Why not YAML? Or JSON? ArchieML differs from other popular formats like YAML and JSON in several areas that we've found are key to making it easy to use: Whitespace is not significant to the document structure In YAML, lines must be indented precisely and variably; the wrong number of spaces to the left of a key invalidates the document, and tabs can't be used. AML ignores all whitespace not within a value. We believe this makes it easier for non-programmers to use, and is essential for use in environments with non-monospaced fonts, like in Google Documents. Unstructured text is ignored; there is no such thing as a parsing error AML was designed so that writers could work in a freeform environment. They should be able to add entire paragraphs as scratch work that do not appear in the output. JSON and YAML have strict schemas that forbid text deviating from a pattern. AML doesn't assume text follows any pattern. If it finds text that looks like data, it treats it as data. Otherwise, it moves on. The notation makes sense to non-programmers Lists of values are noted with bullet points / asterisks, not hyphens or quoted strings that must be separated with commas. An overriding goal was to have a intuitive format that could be passed to a non-technical user — a reporter, an assigning editor or a copy editor — to edit, and to have the format be clear enough that they could make changes without breaking the parsing of the document. If we were using another format, we'd have to explain indentation rules in YAML, or how to match curly braces or properly escape quotation marks in JSON, and so forth. How Does It Work in Practice? For a very simple example, here's a screenshot of the Google Doc that powers a recent graphic about the trick plays used by the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks: To generate the graphic, we load the ArchieML data from the document using the archieml-js npm module , then pass it to an underscore template to render the final markup server-side. This lets the journalists who are focusing on the text and content concentrate on getting the copy in shape independently of the developers working on the graphic. While this is a very simple example, with only a few bits of text and data and one comment at the end that is ignored, when we're covering a breaking news story, we can have a half-dozen people all contributing to a Google Doc at the same time as we gather all the information we need for a graphic and turn it into the final copy blocks that make their way into the finished piece. Resources Parsers and tools in (hopefully) your language of choice. JavaScript Both parsers can be used client-side in the browser, or using Asynchronous Module Definitions (AMD) such as RequireJS, and have test coverage. archieml-js Node Package Manager (npm) archieml-peg (by Jakub Dundalek ) archieml-loader is a Webpack loader for ArchieML files. grunt-archieml (by Andrew Chavez ) gulp-archieml (by Andrew Chavez / The Dallas Morning News) Ruby archieml-ruby is a Ruby parser for ArchieML. It is available through the RubyGems package manager, and has test coverage. RubyGems stream-cms is an elasticsearch backed archieml-to-json manager (by Jacqui Maher / BBC News Labs) R rchie (by Noam Ross ) .NET/C# archieml-net (by Roger Braunstein / Partlyhuman) PHP php-archieml (by Mathieu Gagnon ) Python archieml-python (by Brian Kim ) pip archieml-python (by Kevin Schaul ) Scala SArchieML (by Maciej Biłas ) HTML archieml-element is a Polymer 1.0 component for parsing ArchieML content (by Jay Pilgreen ) Clojure archieclj (by Michael Bauer ) Clojars Google Docs Plugins tools for connecting to Google Drive and parsing documents as ArchieML aml-gdoc-server (by David Yanofsky / Quartz) Node Package Manager (npm) grunt-google-archieml (by Ashlyn Still / The Atlanta Journal-Constitution) Node Package Manager (npm) Fusion Interactive Template (by Kit Cross / Fusion) node-archieml-boilerplate (by Stuart Thompson / The Wall Street Journal) googledoc-to-json (by Brad Oyler ) Node Package Manager (npm) Integrating with Google Documents At The New York Times, we normally write ArchieML in Google Documents. Both parsers include quick-start examples for how to download text from Google Docs and run it through the parser. They also include some formatting steps we take, such as converting links to HTML tags. Examples: JavaScript example Ruby example For more fully-fledged integrations with Google Docs, use one of the plugins above . Introductory Demo Click on any ArchieML textarea to try it out yourself, and see how changes affect the output. Or try out ArchieML in the Sandbox . Keys and values Strings can be stored as part of key/value pairs, defined whenever a line in ArchieML begins with a token followed by a colon. Keys can contain any unicode character, with the exception of whitespace / invisible characters, and a handful of characters that are used within ArchieML ( { } [ ] : . + ). The rest of the string is the value. key: This is a value ☃: Unicode Snowman for you and you and you! Whitespace surrounding keys and values is ignored. Indent as you like. Keys are case sensitive. 1: value 2:value 3 : value 4: value 5: value a: lowercase a A: uppercase A Lines that don't look like keys or other special commands are ignored: This is a key: key: value It's a nice key! Nested key structure Use dot-notation to create nested objects. colors.red: #f00 colors.green: #0f0 colors.blue: #00f You can also use "object" blocks to namespace a group of keys. {colors} red: #f00 green: #0f0 blue: #00f {} {numbers} one: 1 ten: 10 one-hundred: 100 {} key: value Dot notation can be used in object blocks as well: {colors.reds} crimson: #dc143c darkred: #8b0000 {} {colors.blues} cornflowerblue: #6495ed darkblue: #00008b {} You can close an object by beginning a line with {} . ArchieML is parsed one line at a time, so you can also close an object by opening a new one. {colors} red: #f00 green: #0f0 blue: #00f {numbers} one: 1 ten: 10 one-hundred: 100 {} key: value Nested object blocks Object blocks with names prepened with a period nest inside of open objects instead of ending them. Beginning a line with {} closes a nested object and returns to the parent. {colors} red: #f00 green: #0f0 blue: #00f {.numbers} one: 1 ten: 10 one-hundred: 100 {} nestedKey: nestedValue {months} january: 0 february: 1 Arrays of objects Groups of keys can be placed inside an array by giving the array a name within brackets. The name of the array can be any valid key, and can use dot-notation. You can optionally end an array with an empty set of brackets, or by beginning a new array. [scope.array] [] All keys inside the array are inserted into a single object within the array. The parser remembers the first key it found, and whenever it encounters it again, a new object is started. [arrayName] Jeremy spoke with her on Friday, follow-up scheduled for next week name: Amanda age: 26 # Contact: 434-555-1234 name: Tessa age: 30 [] Arrays of strings You can also create "simple" or "flat" arrays of strings. If an asterisk is encountered first within an array, that array will become a simple array, and key/value pairs within it will be ignored. If a key/value pairs is encountered first, then asterisk lines will be ignored. [days] * Sunday note: holiday! * Monday * Tuesday Whitespace is still fine around the '*' * Wednesday * Thursday Friday! * Friday * Saturday [] Nested arrays Array elements can contain arrays of their own. To begin an array while inside an array element, prepend its name with a period. [array] [.subarray] [.subsubarray] key: value Much like nested object blocks, nested arrays must be "closed" with empty brackets in order to move up to the parent level. [days] name: Monday [.tasks] * Clean dishes * Pick up room [] name: Tuesday [.tasks] * Buy milk [] Freeform arrays Freeforms are a third type of array that was created to have better control over presentation from within ArchieML. Unlike regular arrays, which group lines into objects whose values have no order, freeforms preserve the order of each of its lines . Clients that use ArchieML's output can then use that order to render the values, allowing you to vary the presentation for each array item. [+books] kicker: Books you should read score: ★★★★★!!! title: Wuthering Heights author: Emily Brontë title: Middlemarch author: George Eliot score: ★★★★☆ [] Each line becomes its own object , with a type and value . ArchieML splits these two words into separate objects to make it easier to deal with different type of information; rendering logic can always be based on the content of the type attribute. Freeforms also allow you to type unstructured lines of text, which are included as items in the array with a type of text . Note that this means that comments do not work within freeforms. [+text] I can type words here... And separate them into different paragraphs without tags. [] Having full control over order is useful when arrays need to be mixed with other types of data . For example, showing a list of events interspersed with general artwork. [+events] header: My Birthday date: August 20th, 1990 {.image} src: https://example.com/photo.png alt: Family Photo {} header: High School Graduation date: June 4th, 2008 [] Multi-line values Values automatically end when a newline is encountered. But all subsequent text is read into a buffer that can be added to that key. Anchor the end of a multi-line value by following the value with a line beginning with ":end". All whitespace within the block is preserved. Try removing the last line to see how it changes the output: key: value More value Even more value :end Works within object and simple arrays [arrays.complex] key: value more value :end [arrays.simple] * value more value :end Escape characters You can place any text inside of a multi-line value. If one of your lines would be interpreted by the parser as a key or some other special command, you may have to escape that line by adding a backslack to the beginning of it. The backslash won't be included in the value. Try removing the backslashes from the following lines: key: value \:end :end key: value \more: value :end key: value [escaping * is not necessary if we're not inside an array, but will still be removed] \* value :end key: value \:ignore \:skip \:endskip :end Block comments Wrap text between lines that begin with ":skip" and ":endskip" to ignore blocks of text. :skip this: text will: be ignored :endskip There is also a safety mechanism of sorts built in. When the parser encounters a line beginning with ":ignore" (even if it's within a :skip block), parsing immediately stops, and the rest of the document is ignored. key: value :ignore [array] * Blah [] other-key: other value Usage If you use JavaScript or Ruby, we hope you'll try one of the existing ArchieML parsers . If you want to make a parser yourself (or want the technical details on the format), the full specification is online here . Questions or concerns? The Github repository for this site is available at newsdev/archieml.org , and you can use its Issues page to submit questions or bugs on the spec itself. Created by Michael Strickland , Archie Tse , Matthew Ericson and Tom Giratikanon / The New York Times Copyright (c) 2015 The New York Times Company
